name: Power Finance Corporation Ltd
title: Power Finance Corporation Ltd - 532810 - Transcript Of Analyst/Investor Meet Held On May 13, 2026

read.thesis: PFC is a lender, not a capacity operator: FY26 loan book grew only 7% as prepayments hit, FY27 loan growth guided ~10% and spread cut to 2.40–2.50%, while sanctions of INR 2.85 lakh crore sit mostly undisbursed.

summary.headline: PFC FY26 standalone PAT hit a record INR 20,051 crore (+16% YoY), but FY27 spread guided lower at 2.40-2.50% and loan growth at ~10%.
summary.overview: PFC reported its highest-ever standalone net profit of INR 20,051 crore for FY26, up 16% YoY, helped by 13% NII growth and about INR 1,800 crore of provision reversals. Net NPA fell to 0.13% and net credit-impaired ratio to a new low of 0.15%, after resolution of Sinnar Thermal and TRN Energy. Disbursements were INR 1,65,414 crore and loan book grew about 7% to ~INR 5.8 lakh crore, with management blaming elevated prepayments in a falling-rate cycle. Management guided FY27 spread to 2.40-2.50% and loan growth to around 10%, and outlined the proposed PFC-REC merger targeted for 1 April 2027.

financial_highlights.change: of which ~INR 800 crore from Sinnar/TRN resolution, ~INR 1,000 crore from DISCOM ECL reversal

financial_highlights.metric: Yield / cost of funds / spread / NIM FY26

financial_highlights.value: INR 18.55 per share total; final INR 3.95

segments.name: Renewables
segments.commentary: Group renewable book INR 1.65 lakh crore; PFC standalone renewables about 16% of lending. Major FY26 disbursements were hybrid solar-wind; ~INR 16,000 crore sanctioned for battery and pumped storage.

segments.name: Conventional generation
segments.commentary: About 50% of PFC lending now generation, of which 16% renewable and balance conventional (down from ~75% historically). Thermal and nuclear expansion cited as emerging opportunities.

segments.name: Distribution (DISCOMs)
segments.commentary: Lending focused on short- and medium-term DISCOM needs; RBPF short-tenor revolving loans fell as DISCOMs shifted to 3-7 year loans. DISCOM ECL provision reversal of ~INR 1,000 crore on improved ratings; AT&C losses 15.04%; DISCOMs posted first all-India PAT of ~INR 2,700 crore.

guidance_outlook: FY27 spread guided to 2.40%-2.50% (FY26 actual 2.46%), reflecting yield pressure from competitive pricing and forex-driven funding cost.
FY27 loan growth target around 10%; management says without FY26 prepayments growth would have been within the 10-11% guided range.
Management does not expect further RBI rate cuts in FY27 (repo held at 5.25%); expects prepayment pressure to moderate.
PFC-REC merger targeted to take effect 1 April 2027, subject to MCA, RBI, SEBI, cabinet and presidential approvals; government to retain government-company status.
Dividend to follow DIPAM policy of 30% of profit, subject to RBI NBFC dividend rules.
No specific FY27 disbursement guidance; FY26 sanctions INR 2.85 lakh crore with only ~INR 80,000 crore disbursed, so spillover expected.
capex_capacity: India installed capacity crossed 530 GW; about 55 GW non-fossil capacity added in FY26, a record (per management).
Peak power demand hit an all-time high of 256 GW in April 2026.
PFC sanctioned ~INR 16,000 crore cumulatively for battery and pumped storage projects.
Sanctioned-but-undisbursed pool estimated at INR 2.5-3 lakh crore (approximate, per management).
Infrastructure disbursements slow in construction phase; pick-up expected as projects approach commissioning.
demand_pricing: PFC consciously priced new lending competitively in FY26 amid banks' aggressive refinancing of commissioned renewable assets, which drove prepayments.
Banks most willing to refinance renewable portfolios given low gestation, early commissioning, certain cash flows and small ticket sizes.

Forex volatility (rupee depreciation vs USD and EUR, Middle East conflict, trade tariffs) raised FY26 funding costs; hedging covers 97% of USD 10.3 billion foreign currency borrowing, with management saying most mark-to-market losses are notional until maturity.
Borrowing mix: 80:20 domestic-foreign; 65% fixed-rate; 60% bonds, 20% bank term loans, 20% foreign currency (per management).
Repayments from borrowers in FY26 were about INR 1,28,000 crore.

qa_highlights.question: Why did disbursements and loan growth weaken despite stable disbursement volume?
qa_highlights.answer: Management said disbursements were broadly flat (INR 1,65,414 crore vs ~INR 1,68,000 crore) but DISCOMs shifted from short-tenor RBPF revolving loans (~6-month average) to 3-7 year loans, reducing rollover-driven disbursement counts; competition from banks also present.

qa_highlights.question: Why is only a fraction of sanctions disbursed and what is the timing?
qa_highlights.answer: FY26 sanctions were ~INR 2.85 lakh crore with ~INR 80,000 crore disbursed; infrastructure disbursements are slow due to pre-commitment conditions, environmental and land approvals, and pick up near commissioning. Management said the balance is spilling over, not cancelled.

qa_highlights.question: How will the merger affect the government shareholding and borrowing limits?
qa_highlights.answer: Government shareholding would fall to about 41-42% post share swap; management said the government has committed to keep the merged entity a government company, with modalities yet to be decided. Single-borrower exposure limit to banks would fall from 25% to 20% for the merged entity, which management does not see as a challenge.

qa_highlights.question: What is the dividend and ROE outlook post-merger?
qa_highlights.answer: Dividend is 30% of PFC's standalone profit, of which PFC receives REC dividend as income; post-merger dividend will be declared on combined profit under DIPAM's 30% policy, subject to RBI rules. No ROE guidance was given.

qa_highlights.question: How does PFC view the impact of a potential future rate hike?
qa_highlights.answer: About 65% of borrowings are fixed-rate and bond liabilities average 5-6 years, so repricing is gradual; lending rates are linked to the weighted cost of borrowing, so a rate rise would transmit slowly as older debt matures.

qa_highlights.question: Will the FY27 spread decline and what drives it?
qa_highlights.answer: Management guided 2.40-2.50% versus 2.46% in FY26, citing competitive lending rates, prepayment pressure and forex-driven funding costs; the spread is calculated on weighted average cost including foreign borrowings.

risks_watch: Continued prepayments and bank refinancing of commissioned renewable assets could keep loan growth below the ~10% target.
Rupee volatility and Middle East conflict could raise hedging and translation costs on USD 10.3 billion foreign borrowing; ~97% hedged.
Shiga Energy (INR 522 crore) co-lender approval pending within the INR 854 crore of Stage-3 assets resolved outside NCLT.
Stage-3 book of INR 6,323 crore across 19 projects; FY26 provision write-backs (~INR 1,800 crore) will not recur at the same level, so credit cost may rise.
Merger execution: government stake falling below 50%, creditor exposure limits, and workforce integration (about 520 PFC and about 1,000 combined employees per management).
New ECL norms from April 2027 under RBI; management says current policy broadly in sync with RBI IRAC norms.
summary.management_tone: Confident on balance sheet strength, asset quality and the merger timeline, but cautious and somewhat defensive on loan growth, prepayments and spread compression. Management repeatedly deflected on exact disbursement, dividend and ROE figures, and said merger structure details are still under discussion.
key_quotes: Our net credit impaired asset ratio is at new low at 0.15%.
For FY27, we do not expect any further rate cut from RBI.
We are targeting for the merged entity to come into existence by 1st of April 2027.
So, spread is being worked out on the weighted average cost which constitutes both the domestic as well as the foreign borrowings.

growth.why: FY27 loan growth target of around 10% and spread guided lower to 2.40-2.50%, with backing limited to a INR 2.5-3 lakh crore sanctioned-but-undisbursed pool and spillover from FY26 sanctions of INR 2.85 lakh crore, with no specific capacity or timelines given.
